beset.verb type: action — dynamic; the *beset by delays* participle is so common that it works almost adjectivally, naming a condition rather than an event.
beset.transitivity: **transitive** in all three senses — the object is whatever the trouble surrounds (*doubts beset her*, *wolves beset the camp*). The object is obligatory: ✗ *small delays beset*.
beset.passive: **yes**, and the passive is the form you actually meet — *the expedition has been beset by bad weather since Tuesday*, *a crown beset with rubies*.

bet.verb type: action — dynamic in the wagering sense; *I bet she's late* and *you bet* are fixed speech formulas, present tense despite looking like the past.
bet.transitivity: **both** — intransitive (*I never bet*), transitive (*he bet twenty dollars*), ditransitive (*I'll bet you ten dollars*), and it also takes a that-clause.
bet.passive: **restricted** — the money sense passivizes stiffly (*a fortune was bet on that race*), and the idioms have no passive at all: ✗ *that she's late is bet by me*.

broadcast.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, from transmitting a program to scattering seed across a pasture.
broadcast.transitivity: **both** — normally transitive (*NPR broadcast the hearings live*), intransitive when the station itself is the subject (*we broadcast from a studio downtown*).
broadcast.passive: **yes**, and it is the everyday form — *that episode has been broadcast in forty countries*, *the mix had been broadcast over the bare ground before the rain*.

burst.verb type: action — dynamic and sudden throughout; *be bursting with* and *be bursting to* are progressive-only frames.
burst.transitivity: **both**, but overwhelmingly **intransitive** (*the pipe burst*, *she burst into the room*); transitive only in a narrow set — *burst a balloon*, *burst a blood vessel*.
burst.passive: **restricted** — the intransitive senses have no passive at all (✗ *the room was burst into*); the rare transitive allows *a blood vessel was burst by the strain*, but *popped* or *broke* reads better.

bust.verb type: action — dynamic and informal throughout; the participle *busted* doubles as an adjective (*my phone is busted*).
bust.transitivity: **both** — transitive in the break, raid, and demote senses (*they busted the lock*, *vice busted that club*), intransitive of a couple in *bust up* (*they busted up over money*).
bust.passive: **yes**, and the *get*-passive is the commonest form — *he got busted for driving without a license*, *two sergeants have been busted since the investigation opened*.

cast.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, literal and figurative alike; the participle is adjectival in *cast iron*.
cast.transitivity: **both** — overwhelmingly transitive (*cast a ballot*, *cast an unknown actor as the lead*); intransitive with a particle (*we cast off at dawn*, *she cast about for a polite way to say no*).
cast.passive: **yes** — *the bell was cast in a foundry outside Cincinnati*, *the whole film had been cast before the script was finished*.

clear-cut.verb type: action — dynamic, and purely a forestry verb; the common adjective *a clear-cut case of fraud* is a separate word that never behaves like it.
clear-cut.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is the tract of forest (*loggers clear-cut that ridge*); it drops only when the practice itself is meant (*the company clear-cuts about a thousand acres a year*).
clear-cut.passive: **yes**, and it is the usual form in reporting — *half the watershed has been clear-cut since the mill reopened*.

cost.verb type: **stative** in the price and loss senses — a property of the thing, not an act, and it rejects the progressive: ✗ *the ticket is costing ninety dollars*. Only the accounting sense (*costed the job*) is a true action verb.
cost.transitivity: **transitive** with an amount (*the repair cost four hundred dollars*), and **ditransitive** with the person first (*it cost him the promotion*, *that mistake has cost us two customers*).
cost.passive: **no** in the price and loss senses — ✗ *four hundred dollars was cost by the repair*, ✗ *the promotion was cost him*. Only the dynamic accounting sense passivizes: *the job was costed at twelve thousand dollars*.

crosscut.verb type: action — dynamic; the -ing form has hardened into an adjective in policy writing (*crosscutting concerns*, *crosscutting cleavages*).
crosscut.transitivity: **both** — transitive on a board, a scene, or a set of categories (*he crosscut the plank*, *these loyalties crosscut every party line*), intransitive of how a tool behaves and in *crosscut between two conversations*.
crosscut.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the chase had been crosscut with shots of the empty house*.

cut.verb type: action — dynamic throughout, literal and figurative; the participle serves as an adjective in *a cut lip*.
cut.transitivity: **both** — normally transitive (*she cut the rope*, *they cut the budget twice*), intransitive of an engine or a person moving in (*the motor cut out*, *a pickup cut in front of us*).
cut.passive: **yes** — *the chapter has been cut down to four pages*, *the whole valley had been cut off by morning*, *I got my hair cut*.

downcast.verb type: action — dynamic, but archaic as a verb; in living English *downcast* is a participle-adjective (*downcast eyes*, *he looked downcast*).
downcast.transitivity: **transitive** in both senses — the object is the eyes or the person dispirited (*she downcast her eyes*, *the verdict downcast everyone*).
downcast.passive: **restricted** — a passive is buildable (*the whole town was downcast by the news*) but reads as the adjective; modern American English says *was discouraged* or *was depressed*.

english.verb type: action — dynamic, and archaic: a scholar's word for the act of translating, written with a small e.
english.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is the text being translated (*english the Old Norse sagas*), and it is obligatory.
english.passive: **yes** — *most of the popular French romances had been englished by 1700* — though a modern writer would say *translated into English*.

fit.verb type: **stative** in the core senses — being the right size or suiting something is a property, not an act, and it resists the progressive: ✗ *these jeans are fitting me*. The install and tailor senses (*fitted the room with sprinklers*) are ordinary action verbs.
fit.transitivity: **both** — transitive in *the key fit the lock* and *the tailor fitted the jacket*, intransitive with a place phrase (*six people fit in that car*, *he never fit in at that school*).
fit.passive: **no** in the stative senses — ✗ *the lock was fit by the key*, ✗ *I am not fit by anything in that closet*. **Yes** in the dynamic ones: *the van has been fitted with a lift*, *she has been fitted for a brace twice this year*.

forecast.verb type: action — dynamic; sense 3 (*the early strikes forecast a long winter*) shades toward the stative 'foreshadow', where an event simply points to what follows.
forecast.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is the prediction, a noun phrase or a that-clause (*analysts forecast a slowdown*, *the service forecasts snow above five thousand feet*).
forecast.passive: **yes**, and it is the default when no forecaster is named — *rain was forecast for Thursday afternoon*.

hit.verb type: action — dynamic and sudden; a large family of fixed idioms (*hit the road*, *hit it off*, *hit the roof*) rides on the same verb.
hit.transitivity: **transitive** in nearly every sense, with the object obligatory (*hit the ball*, *gas prices have hit five dollars*); intransitive only inside phrasal frames like *hit back* and *hit out*.
hit.passive: **yes** — *she was hit by a car*, *two deer have been hit on that stretch this month*. The idioms refuse it: ✗ *it off was hit by them at the wedding*.

hoist.verb type: action — dynamic; the invariant participle survives only in the frozen *hoist with his own petard*.
hoist.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is the heavy thing raised (*they hoisted the piano through a third-floor window*), and it is obligatory.
hoist.passive: **yes** — *the banner has been hoisted over the entrance since Friday*, and the idiom is passive by definition: *he was hoist with his own petard*.

hurt.verb type: **both** — action in *I hurt my back* and *the scandal hurt the company*, but the intransitive *my knee hurts* names a state (it still takes the progressive: *my knee is hurting*). *Be hurting* for money is progressive-only.
hurt.transitivity: **both** — intransitive with the body part as subject (*my shoulder hurts when it rains*), transitive with a person, a feeling, or a thing as object (*it hurt her*, *skipping practice hurts the whole team*).
hurt.passive: **restricted** — *nobody has been hurt at that intersection* is standard, but the participle there is closer to the adjective *injured* than to a true passive, and the intransitive *my knee hurts* has no passive at all.

input.verb type: action — dynamic; the noun *input* is far commoner than the verb, which stays in computing and business writing.
input.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is the data (*input the account number before you hit save*), and it is obligatory.
input.passive: **yes** — *the wrong shipping address has been input* — though *entered* or *typed in* usually reads better in the same slot.

inset.verb type: action — dynamic; in practice the participle does most of the work as an adjective (*an inset panel*).
inset.transitivity: **transitive**, normally with a place phrase — *inset the shelves into the wall*, *inset a detail map in the lower corner*.
inset.passive: **yes**, and it is the usual form — *a photograph of the author has been inset on the back cover*.

intercut.verb type: action — dynamic; film and video editing vocabulary, extended to writing and performance.
intercut.transitivity: **transitive** — the frame is *intercut A with B* or *intercut between* two lines of action (*she intercut the wedding scene with shots of the empty church*).
intercut.passive: **yes** — *the trailer has been intercut with clips from the sequel*.

knit.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense; the participle is adjectival in *a tightly knit family* and *a close-knit town*.
knit.transitivity: **both** — transitive with yarn, brows, or people (*she knitted a scarf*, *he knit his brows*), intransitive of a healing bone (*the fracture knit faster than the doctor expected*).
knit.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the interviews had been knit together into a single narrative*. The bone sense is intransitive and has none: ✗ *the bone was knit cleanly by itself*.

let.verb type: action — dynamic and causative, taking a bare infinitive after its object (*let me go*, never ✗ *let me to go*); *let's* is a frozen first-person imperative formula.
let.transitivity: **transitive** — object plus a bare infinitive or a particle (*let the dog out*, *let forty people go*); the object is obligatory: ✗ *he lets*.
let.passive: **restricted** — the causative has no ordinary passive (✗ *he was let stay out past ten*; say *was allowed to stay*), but the fixed phrasal and rental uses do passivize: *forty people were let go*, *the cottage has been let every summer since 1990*.

miscast.verb type: action — dynamic, and met almost entirely as a passive participle.
miscast.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is the actor, the person, or the issue (*the studio miscast the lead*, *critics miscast the study*).
miscast.passive: **yes**, and it is the normal form — *he was badly miscast as the villain*, *the bill has been miscast as a tax increase*.

misread.verb type: action — dynamic in both the literal and the figurative sense.
misread.transitivity: **transitive** — object obligatory in practice (*misread the label*, *misread the market*, *misread politeness as agreement*).
misread.passive: **yes** — *the altimeter had been misread in the fog* — though the active, with the person who erred as subject, is far commoner.

offset.verb type: action — dynamic, though *a federal credit offsets part of the cost* states a standing relationship as much as an event.
offset.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is what gets balanced out (*offset capital losses against gains*, *the airline offsets every flight it sells*).
offset.passive: **yes** — *most of the savings were offset by higher fuel prices*, *the chimney had been offset a foot from center*.

output.verb type: action — dynamic; like *input*, the noun is much commoner than the verb, and the verb means 'produce' or 'send out', not 'go out'.
output.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is what the machine or plant produces (*the script outputs a CSV file to the same folder*).
output.passive: **restricted** — grammatical but clumsy (*the same error has been output twice*); careful writing reaches for *produced*, *written*, or *returned* instead.

overstay.verb type: action — dynamic, and a regular verb (*overstayed*) in real American English despite the invariant listing.
overstay.transitivity: **both** — normally transitive with a fixed object (*overstay your welcome*, *overstay a visa*), intransitive of lingering (*nobody wants to overstay at a party that has clearly ended*).
overstay.passive: **no** in real use — the object is a possessed noun, which blocks it: ✗ *his welcome was overstayed*, ✗ *the visa was overstayed by him*.

proofread.verb type: action — dynamic; one careful pass over a text rather than a state.
proofread.transitivity: **both** — transitive with the text as object (*would you proofread this paragraph?*), intransitive of the job itself (*she proofreads for a living*).
proofread.passive: **yes** — *the manuscript has been proofread by two editors*, *every page has been proofread against the marked-up copy*.

put.verb type: action — dynamic; it needs a place or manner complement as much as it needs an object.
put.transitivity: **transitive**, and the object alone is not enough: ✗ *put the milk* — *put the milk back in the refrigerator*. In the three-word *put up with*, the object follows the whole phrase: ✗ *put the noise up with*.
put.passive: **yes** — *the proposal had been put to the board twice already*, *my chair has been put out in the hallway*.

quit.verb type: action — dynamic; it takes an -ing complement, never an infinitive: ✗ *quit to smoke*.
quit.transitivity: **both** — transitive with a job, an activity, or a program (*she quit her job*, *quit checking your phone*), intransitive when what is given up is understood (*three people have quit since the new manager arrived*).
quit.passive: **restricted** — barely used: ✗ *her job was quit the week after the merger*. Even the computing sense prefers *the app was closed* to *was quit*.

read.verb type: action — dynamic in the core senses; senses 4 and 5 (*that line reads as sarcastic*, *the sign reads 'No entry after six'*) are **stative** — how a text stands, not something anyone does.
read.transitivity: **both** — transitive (*I read two newspapers every morning*), ditransitive (*he read the kids a story*), and intransitive in *read as / read like* and in *she reads every night*.
read.passive: **yes** in the ordinary senses — *the meter has been read already*, *the whole list had been read aloud*. **No** in senses 4 and 5: ✗ *sarcastic is read as by that line*, ✗ *'No entry' is read by the sign*.

rebroadcast.verb type: action — dynamic; broadcast-industry vocabulary, where ordinary speech says *replay* or *air again*.
rebroadcast.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is the program or the signal (*the tower rebroadcasts the signal to the far side of the valley*).
rebroadcast.passive: **yes** — *the concert has been rebroadcast every December since 1998*.

recast.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: replacing an actor, reworking an argument, melting metal down again.
recast.transitivity: **transitive** — an actor, a proposal, or a casting (*she recasts every complaint as a question*).
recast.passive: **yes**, and it is usual in the film sense — *the part has been recast twice since the read-through*, *the bronze has been recast three times over the centuries*.

refit.verb type: action — dynamic; American English normally uses the regular *refitted*, and the invariant *refit* is mostly the noun.
refit.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is the ship, building, or part (*the mechanic refitted the panel*, *the yard refits two ferries every winter*).
refit.passive: **yes** — *the trawler has been refitted twice since it was launched*.

reread.verb type: action — dynamic, in both the literal and the critical sense.
reread.transitivity: **both** — transitive (*she reread the email four times*), intransitive when the object is obvious (*it helps to reread a hard paragraph out loud*).
reread.passive: **yes** — *the novel has been reread as a book about class, not romance* — though the active dominates.

reset.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, from routers and passwords to relationships and broken bones.
reset.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is what returns to its starting state (*reset the router*, *this switch resets the counter to zero*).
reset.passive: **yes** — *every machine on the floor has been reset*, *the break had been reset badly the first time*.

retrofit.verb type: action — dynamic; American engineering writing strongly prefers the regular *retrofitted*.
retrofit.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is the existing structure or system, usually with *with* (*they retrofitted the building with sprinklers in 2014*).
retrofit.passive: **yes**, and it is the common form — *half the fleet has been retrofitted with cleaner engines*.

rid.verb type: action — dynamic, but it barely stands alone: it lives in *rid X of Y*, in *get rid of*, and in the **stative** *be rid of*, which names the resulting state rather than the act.
rid.transitivity: **transitive**, and it demands an *of*-phrase: *rid the basement of that smell*, ✗ *rid the basement*. Often reflexive — *he had rid himself of every reminder*.
rid.passive: **restricted** — a true passive (*the department was rid of its worst habits*) is stiff and rare; what learners meet instead is *get rid of* and *be rid of*, fixed frames where *rid* is a participle but not a passive.

set.verb type: action — dynamic; it also has a genuine intransitive life in *the sun set* and *let the concrete set*, where nothing is acted on at all.
set.transitivity: **both** — transitive by default, and the object is obligatory, unlike *sit*: *set the box on the table*, ✗ *set down and rest*. Intransitive of the sun going down and of concrete, glue, or gelatin hardening.
set.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the film is set in a small town in Maine*, *bail was set at ten thousand dollars*. No passive for the sun or the concrete: ✗ *the ridge was set behind by the sun*.

shed.verb type: action — dynamic; sense 5 (*this jacket sheds rain but not wind*) states a standing property rather than an event.
shed.transitivity: **transitive** — hair, leaves, weight, jobs, tears, blood, or water (*the company shed four hundred jobs last quarter*).
shed.passive: **yes** — *plenty of blood had been shed over that border already*, *not a tear was shed*. The idiom *shed light on* stays active.

shit.verb type: action — dynamic and vulgar; barred from writing that matters.
shit.transitivity: **both** — intransitive in the literal sense (*the dog shit on the neighbor's lawn*), transitive in the fixed *shit oneself* and *shit a brick*, and prepositional in *shit on someone*.
shit.passive: **restricted** — only the prepositional passive works: *nobody deserves to be shit on like that*. The literal intransitive has no passive.

shred.verb type: action — dynamic; American English treats it as a regular verb (*shredded*) in nearly every sentence.
shred.transitivity: **both** — transitive of documents, cheese, or an argument (*the defense shredded the witness's timeline*), intransitive of fabric and tires coming apart (*cheap tires shred on gravel roads*) and of the slang *that kid can really shred*.
shred.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *six boxes of old files have been shredded*. The intransitive coming-apart and slang senses have none.

shut.verb type: action — dynamic; unlike *close* it will not stand in front of a noun as an adjective: *a closed door*, ✗ *a shut door*.
shut.transitivity: **both** — transitive (*shut the window*, *they shut down two plants*), intransitive of a business closing (*the diner shuts at nine on weeknights*).
shut.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the interstate has been shut down twice this month*, *the dog had been shut up in the garage all afternoon*.

sight-read.verb type: action — dynamic; a musician's skill word and nothing else.
sight-read.transitivity: **both** — transitive with the music as object (*she sight-read the whole sonata at the audition*), intransitive of the ability itself (*you have to practice to sight-read well*).
sight-read.passive: **restricted** — grammatical (*the part had been sight-read once and then recorded*) but rare, since the performer is normally the subject.

simulcast.verb type: action — dynamic; a blend of *simultaneous* and *broadcast* that inherits both the forms and the sense.
simulcast.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is the program or event (*the station simulcasts the game on AM and FM*).
simulcast.passive: **yes** — *the concert has been simulcast to theaters nationwide*.

slit.verb type: action — dynamic and sudden: one long narrow cut, not a break into parts.
slit.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is obligatory (*slit the bag open along the top*, *this blade slits plastic wrap cleanly*).
slit.passive: **yes** — *the animal's throat had been slit cleanly*, *someone has slit the seam on this cushion*.

split.verb type: action — dynamic; the -ing form is an intensifying adjective in *a splitting headache*.
split.transitivity: **both** — transitive (*let's split the check*, *the vote split the town down the middle*), intransitive of something breaking or people parting (*the log had split along an old crack*, *they split up after eleven years*).
split.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *profits are split evenly among the partners*, *the difference has been split*. No passive for the slang *we split around midnight*.

spread.verb type: action — dynamic in both directions: something spreads on its own, or somebody spreads it.
spread.transitivity: **both** — intransitive of fire, disease, and rumors (*the fire spread faster than anyone expected*), transitive of butter, blankets, news, and payments (*we spread the payments over eighteen months*).
spread.passive: **yes** for the transitive senses — *the news has been spread already*, *the work has been spread across three visits*. **No** for the intransitive: ✗ *eleven counties have been spread to by the virus*.

sublet.verb type: action — dynamic; it takes its forms and its meaning from *let* in the rent-out sense.
sublet.transitivity: **both** — transitive (*he sublet his studio to a friend*), intransitive when the practice itself is meant (*my lease says I can't sublet at all*).
sublet.passive: **yes** — *most of the finish work had been sublet to a smaller firm*.

sweat.verb type: action — dynamic, though perspiring is a bodily process rather than a chosen act; it takes the progressive freely (*he's sweating through his shirt*).
sweat.transitivity: **both** — mostly intransitive (*I sweat buckets on that hike*, *the glass sweats in this humidity*), transitive in *don't sweat it*, *sweat blood*, *sweat it out*, and the cooking *sweat the onions in butter*.
sweat.passive: **restricted** — only the cooking sense passivizes naturally (*the leeks were sweated before the stock went in*); the idioms refuse it (✗ *the small stuff shouldn't be sweated*) and the intransitive has no passive.

telecast.verb type: action — dynamic, and dated; American English now says *broadcast*, *air*, or *televise*.
telecast.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is the program or event (*CBS telecasts the tournament every April*).
telecast.passive: **yes** — *the game has been telecast in prime time twice this season*, *the ceremony had been telecast live*.

thrust.verb type: action — dynamic and sudden; sense 5 (*a rock ledge thrusts out over the valley*) is **stative** — the shape of a push, held still.
thrust.transitivity: **both** — transitive with a direction phrase (*he thrust his hands into his pockets*), intransitive in the fencing and protruding senses (*the pier thrust two hundred feet into the lake*).
thrust.passive: **yes**, and *be thrust into* is the commonest frame of all — *she was thrust into the lead role two days before opening*, *responsibility thrust upon them at nineteen*.

typecast.verb type: action — dynamic, and met almost entirely as a passive participle.
typecast.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is the actor or the person being labeled (*Hollywood typecasts character actors within about two films*).
typecast.passive: **yes**, and it is the default — *he was typecast as the villain*, *she has been typecast as the tough boss in every series since*.

undercut.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: pricing, undermining, and cutting away from below.
undercut.transitivity: **transitive** — a rival, an argument, or a riverbank (*their online store undercuts every shop in town*).
undercut.passive: **yes** — *the whole industry has been undercut by cheap imports*, *the bank had been undercut until the tree fell in*.

uppercut.verb type: action — dynamic; boxing shorthand, and the noun *a left uppercut* does nearly all the work.
uppercut.transitivity: **both** — transitive with the opponent as object (*she uppercut him twice in the final round*), intransitive of the technique (*he uppercuts whenever his opponent drops a shoulder*).
uppercut.passive: **restricted** — buildable but almost never written (*he was uppercut into the ropes*); boxing writing keeps the puncher as the subject.

upset.verb type: action — dynamic and causative (*it upsets her when people are late*); the participle is a true adjective in *he looked upset*, stressed up-SET.
upset.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is the person, the stomach, the thing knocked over, the favorite, or the plan (*a tenth seed had upset the champion*).
upset.passive: **yes** — *the incumbent was upset by an unknown candidate*, *decades of settled practice have been upset*. Note that *she was upset* is usually the adjective, not a passive.

wed.verb type: action — dynamic; dated outside headlines, and *wedded* survives mainly as an adjective (*wedded bliss*, *too wedded to the old process*).
wed.transitivity: **both** — intransitive of the couple (*they wed in a courthouse ceremony last fall*), transitive of the officiant or of joining two things (*the same judge wed both of my sisters*, *a good design weds comfort to durability*).
wed.passive: **restricted** — the officiant sense passivizes (*half the couples in that town have been wedded by a retired chaplain*) but sounds archaic; *be wedded to an idea* is the adjective, not a passive.

wet.verb type: action — dynamic, and far commoner as an adjective than as a verb.
wet.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is what gets wet, often reflexive or a fixed noun (*wet the brush*, *he nearly wet himself*, *the toddler wet the bed*).
wet.passive: **yes** — *the slide was wetted with a drop of saline*, *the whole stack of newspapers has been wet by the rain* — though in speech people say *got wet*.
